results.name: two_example_dip
results.description: Yes-rate on 2-example sets minus the mean yes-rate on 3- and 4-example sets; observed < null means people are more conservative on two-example sets (relative to larger sets) than the model's monotone capacity limit predicts.

results.name: lag1_response_repetition
results.description: Proportion of consecutive trials (same participant, trial_index increasing by 1) with the same response as the previous trial; observed > null means people perseverate on their previous answer beyond what stimulus-driven model predictions produce.

results.name: out_of_range_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate for targets lying outside [min, max] of the examples by more than 5; observed > null means people extend generalization beyond the example range more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: out_of_range_yes_rate
# description: For sets of 2+ examples, yes-rate for targets lying outside [min, max] of the examples by more than 5; observed > null means people extend generalization beyond the example range more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = (n >= 2) & ((t < lo - 5) | (t > hi + 5))
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[sel].mean())

results.name: recency_nearest_example
results.description: For 2+ example sets and non-member targets, yes-rate when the nearest example is the last one shown minus when it is the first one shown; nonzero observed vs a ~0 null means presentation order (recency/primacy) matters, which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: recency_nearest_example
# description: For 2+ example sets and non-member targets, yes-rate when the nearest example is the last one shown minus when it is the first one shown; nonzero observed vs a ~0 null means presentation order (recency/primacy) matters, which the order-invariant model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    d = np.where(np.isnan(d), np.inf, d)
    idx = np.argmin(d, axis=1)
    mind = d[np.arange(len(t)), idx]
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ok = (n >= 2) & (mind > 0)
    last = ok & (idx == n - 1)
    first = ok & (idx == 0)
    if last.sum() == 0 or first.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[last].mean() - r[first].mean())

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials with trial_index >= 225 minus yes-rate on trials with trial_index < 225; observed differing from null means a drift in yes-bias across the session that the stationary model does not capture (observed < null: people become more conservative over time).

results.name: near_vs_far_distance_gradient
results.description: Among targets not in the set, yes-rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 10 from the nearest example; observed > null means people show a steeper numerical-similarity gradient than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: near_vs_far_distance_gradient
# description: Among targets not in the set, yes-rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 10 from the nearest example; observed > null means people show a steeper numerical-similarity gradient than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    near = (dist > 0) & (dist <= 3)
    far = dist > 10
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: singleton_yes_rate_far_targets
results.description: For single-example sets, yes-rate for targets more than 10 away from the example; observed > null means people generalize from one example more broadly (via rules/broad similarity) than the model predicts, observed < null means more narrowly.
results.code:
# name: singleton_yes_rate_far_targets
# description: For single-example sets, yes-rate for targets more than 10 away from the example; observed > null means people generalize from one example more broadly (via rules/broad similarity) than the model predicts, observed < null means more narrowly.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0")).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = single.to_numpy() & (np.abs(t - x) > 10)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[sel].mean())

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: For multi-example sets whose examples all share one parity, yes-rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means people rely on parity more strongly than the model predicts (observed < null: less).
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: For multi-example sets whose examples all share one parity, yes-rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null means people rely on parity more strongly than the model predicts (observed < null: less).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    allodd = np.nansum(par == 1, axis=1) == n
    alleven = np.nansum(par == 0, axis=1) == n
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = (n >= 2) & (allodd | alleven)
    setpar = np.where(allodd, 1, 0)
    same = sel & ((t % 2) == setpar)
    opp = sel & ((t % 2) != setpar)
    if same.sum() == 0 or opp.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[opp].mean())
